newsitem.title: USA: US natgas,power company mergers forge new industry.
newsitem.headline: US natgas,power company mergers forge new industry.

text.p: Electricity and natural gas companies are beating a path to each other's doors as they seek alliances to help them face open competition.

Deregulation threatens to erode utilities' traditional profit base, with several states already ripping out regulated prices and replacing them with competitive pilot programs, allowing consumers to pick where they buy their power.
"They are looking for sources of new earnings growth and expanding their services mix," said Barry Abramson, Prudential Securities Inc's senior utilities analyst.

This move has spawned a flood of strategic mergers between gas and power companies over the past 18 months, with the aggregate annual revenues of companies already in mergers now totalling more than $30 billion.
Ed Tirello, senior vice-president at NatWest Securities estimated another 10 such mergers could be announced in 1997.

If state and federal regulators approve all these pending mergers, they will spawn a new industry of huge, one-stop shops for natural gas and power, freeing customers from their traditional dependence on just one or two local utilities.
The trend is likely to continue.
"This is just the tip of the iceberg," said Peter Fusaro, president of Global Change Associates.
"Every one of the gas companies is a target. A lot of electric utilities are looking," Abramson said.
And the list of potential suitors is lengthy. There are more than 140 investor-owned electric utilities in the U.S.

Enron and Portland General's planned merger and a merger between Duke and PanEnergy highlight this new bond between gas and power, Abramson said. "The electric and gas convergence was going to happen faster than once thought."
Gas firms believe they can bring valuable insights to a utility partnership based on experiences from adjusting to deregulation of their own industry over the past decade.

They also see power as a lucrative growth area, with gas boosting its current 20 percent share of the power generation market, analysts said. In fact, Enron and PanEnergy now have subsidiaries that market wholesale power nationwide.
"They are both strong companies. They are going to help each other out," said Gruntal & Co analyst Penelope Adelmann, referring to the Duke and PanEnergy merger.

Gas firms could cross-sell their products and services to electric utility customers, analysts said. "You can market gas services to LILCO customers. It's a natural prospect list," Adelmann said, citing the Long Island Lighting Co (LILCO) and Brooklyn Union deal, which was announced in December.
For electric utilities, healthy gas partners can shore up their balance sheets.

Some, like LILCO, with its Shoreham nuclear liabilities, are saddled with debts tied to uneconomic investments from back in the days of regulated electricity prices, when the cost of such projects was passed down to consumers.
